If you shop according to unit price, which where I live is listed in smaller print somewhere on the price tag, you can avoid being tricked by excessive packaging, stick to your budget easier, and generally just have a more enjoyable time grocery shopping. You can buy whatever you want as long as it is at or below your target unit price.

As an example, my grocery spending has been averaging about $250 per month and my target unit price has been around 13-cents per ounce. I often get foods that are around 10-cents per ounce and will buy a few items, usually snacks, that are as much as 26-cents per ounce as the lower unit price of my other food offsets the higher food. The more expensive foods are usually sweets and treats. After a while of doing this you will get a pretty good idea of what you can offset and what your running average cost per ounce is. Sometimes I spend waaay more than I intended on spending on a grocery trip, but since I've stuck to my target unit price I know that even though I've spent more money, I've got much more food. If you've spent twice as much as your budget allows for a single month and stuck to your target unit price you will not have any grocery expense for the following month.

Some things require you to add water and, as a result, their cost per weight is off. You'll have to just do your best to determine whether you can afford that sort of food. You should also be aware that some stores do a better job of listing the correct unit price on the price tag. If you stick to this sort of grocery shopping you'll be able to spot ones that seem a little 'off' and do some quick math to find out what the correct unit price is. Finally, you would be surprised how often the larger, bulk items are actually more expensive than the smaller, single-serving containers of the same product. Spaghetti-Os are, 100% of the time for me, cheaper in the smaller cans than the larger cans.

I hope this helps someone out there!
Tip: Shop for groceries according to unit price instead of total price.

A bunch of my friends hosted for a few years. A lot of my friends also used it to stay in different places around the globe. Basically, AirBNB can come in a bunch of different varieties.

  1. The person you are staying with is around, and they enjoy hosting. They'll usually show you around town, chill with you in the evening, and if you're lucky they'll be pretty quirky and interesting. Imaging getting to live with a cool character for a few days. You'll likely have a lot of stories to tell afterwards.

  2. The person is mia for most of you being there. In some cases instead of renting a place for example the host will just AirBNB their lodge. Usually these places are bit more expensive, but you do get to stay in some pretty cool houses. And it's usually still less expensive than comparative hotels.

  3. The host doesn't give a fuck. I've never heard of a story like this, but I'd imagine there are times when a host doesn't vibe with you, doesn't care, etc. However AirBNB is pretty good with their ratings/reviews so you can quickly figure stuff like this out beforehand. The very process allows you to roughly know what you're getting into.

Overall, I like the service. I mostly travel using hostels, since I like having large groups of other travelers to mingle with, but in smaller cities, or when you want a more personal experience, I can see AirBNB being pretty cool.
